reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Occurs in the setting of portal hypertension and is recognised endoscopically by a snake-skin (mosaic) mucosal pattern, most prominent in the gastric body and fundus
Severe disease shows discrete red or brown spots superimposed on the mosaic pattern, reflecting more advanced congestion
Must be distinguished from gastric antral vascular ectasia, which produces linear red stripes (watermelon stomach) concentrated in the antrum and is not driven by portal pressure
Usually causes chronic, slow blood loss with iron-deficiency anaemia, though acute overt bleeding can occur
Severity often parallels the degree of portal hypertension and may worsen after obliteration of oesophageal varices

Management is directed at lowering portal pressure with non-selective beta-blockers, and refractory bleeding may respond to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting or measures to treat the underlying liver disease
Iron supplementation and, where needed, transfusion address the resulting anaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Portal hypertensive gastropathy results from the passive congestion of the gastric mucosal and submucosal microvasculature that accompanies raised portal venous pressure, usually from cirrhosis. Dilatation of mucosal capillaries and venules, with ectasia and oedema but relatively little inflammation, produces the characteristic mosaic or snake-skin appearance, and the fragile congested mucosa bleeds easily. The severity tends to track with the degree of portal hypertension, and it may become more apparent after endoscopic eradication of oesophageal varices diverts flow into the gastric mucosal bed.
additionalDifferentials: Erosive or reactive gastropathy from drugs or alcohol
Dieulafoy lesion as a source of obscure bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to identify the mosaic pattern and grade severity, and to distinguish it from antral vascular ectasia
Full blood count and iron studies to quantify chronic blood loss
Liver function tests and assessment of the underlying liver disease and its severity
Imaging of the portal system (Doppler ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging) to confirm portal hypertension
Measurement of the hepatic venous pressure gradient in selected cases
Faecal occult blood testing where occult loss is suspected
redFlags: Acute overt upper gastrointestinal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
Rapidly falling haemoglobin or transfusion dependence
Signs of decompensated liver disease accompanying the bleeding
reference.prognosis: Portal hypertensive gastropathy is usually a chronic source of low-grade blood loss that is manageable, but its course mirrors the underlying liver disease and portal hypertension; severe or refractory bleeding carries a worse outlook and depends on control of portal pressure.
pitfalls: Misclassifying antral vascular ectasia as portal hypertensive gastropathy, since the two require different treatment
Expecting portal-pressure-lowering therapy to help antral vascular ectasia, which it does not
Overlooking the tendency for the gastropathy to worsen after variceal obliteration
Attributing anaemia solely to varices and missing ongoing mucosal loss
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Non-selective beta-blockade with propranolol or carvedilol to lower portal pressure, the mainstay for reducing chronic and recurrent bleeding
Iron replacement, oral or intravenous, and blood transfusion as needed to correct iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic mucosal blood loss
Treatment of the underlying liver disease, whose severity drives the course
Acute overt bleeding managed with resuscitation and vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictors
Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt or a surgical shunt for refractory or transfusion-dependent bleeding
Endoscopic distinction from gastric antral vascular ectasia, which requires endoscopic ablation such as argon plasma coagulation rather than portal-pressure reduction
